Q: How to implement Hilt correctly? A:

Here is how to fix your setup step-by-step.

1. Fix the KSP Version

In your libs.versions.toml, your Kotlin version is 2.2.10, but your KSP version is 2.3.4. KSP versions must match your Kotlin version exactly.

Change your libs.versions.toml:

[versions]
# ... other versions
kotlin = "2.2.10"
# KSP must start with the Kotlin version it supports
ksp = "2.2.10-1.0.27" 
hilt = "2.57.2"

2. Update Project-level build.gradle.kts

Ensure your Hilt plugin is correctly defined here. You have it correct, but make sure no other Hilt-related lines are lingering.

plugins {
    alias(libs.plugins.android.application) apply false
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.compose) apply false
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.android) apply false
    alias(libs.plugins.ksp) apply false
    alias(libs.plugins.hilt) apply false // Keep this as apply false
}

3. Update App-level build.gradle.kts

The error "already requested at line 2" often occurs if you try to provide a version in the app module when it was already defined in the project-level file. Since you are using alias, you should not have a version in the plugins block here.

Clean up your plugins block like this:

plugins {
    alias(libs.plugins.android.application)
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.android) // This is required for Hilt
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.compose)
    alias(libs.plugins.ksp)
    alias(libs.plugins.hilt) // Uncomment this
}

4. Final Verification

Check your dependencies block one last time. You are using KSP for the compiler, which is correct for modern Hilt setups:

dependencies {
    // ... other deps
    
    // Hilt
    implementation(libs.hilt.android)
    ksp(libs.hilt.compiler) 
}

If you still see the "Already requested" error after these changes, go to File > Invalidate Caches... and restart Android Studio. Sometimes Gradle's configuration cache gets stuck on a previous failed attempt.

Q: Core dumped, but the core file is not in the current directory A:

A one-liner to get the latest core dump path:

ls -t $(cat /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern | awk -F% '{print $1"*"}') 2>/dev/null | head -1

You can of course modify the last -1 on that line to, e.g., -4 to get the last four core dumps.

Note: That's not expected to work, e.g., in case the path pattern uses variables before the last / or when non core dump files are in that directory.

Q: Redirect I/O inside a shell script A:

Putting the variables inside "" solves the problem:

echo "Expanding CSS files..."
for css in `find . -type f -name \*.css -print`
do
   echo "Expanding $css"
   temp="$css.tmp"
   cp $css $temp
   ./node_modules/.bin/beautifier "$temp" > "$css" 
   rm $temp
   
done

The real problem was there weren’t any spaces between >. But as Biffen pointed out, this is a good practice. If the line were like this,

"$temp">"$css"

An error raises:

unexpected EOF while looking for matching `"'
syntax error: unexpected end of file

So it's easier to debug.

Although my answer works, Biffen has discovered the real error, and the credit should go to him.
